comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C66-C69, C122 regarding treatment engagement metrics. Both find these null findings support the interpretation that symptom change, not treatment exposure, drives metacognitive changes. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, peer reviewers accept without challenge.

Strong agreement on primary longitudinal findings (C7-C8, C61-C62, C99, C141). Both acknowledge the statistical significance (p<0.001) and accept the evidence for correlated changes in symptoms and confidence. OpenEval and peer reviewers both rate as SUPPORTED despite small effect sizes.

Complete agreement on baseline cross-sectional replication (C58-C60, C105-C107). Both explicitly acknowledge this replicates prior work showing heightened confidence in compulsivity and lowered confidence in anxious-depression. Both rate as SUPPORTED with no concerns raised.

Strong agreement on uncertainty regarding treatment-specific effects (C11-C13, C86-C88, C115-C116). Both note the non-significant interaction undermines claims of differential effects across treatment groups. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to limited power; peer reviewers express similar concerns about practice effects and lack of interaction.

Agreement on the association between symptom and confidence changes (C9-C10, C70, C100), but both emphasize weakness of effect. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with caution about weak correlation (r=-0.12); peer reviewers similarly note 'weak link' and question clinical relevance despite accepting the finding.

Disagreement on confidence that performance controls rule out practice effects (C63-C65, C101-C102). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, viewing staircasing procedure as critical strength. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether practice effects are truly ruled out despite the controls.

Agreement on exploratory findings (C76-C78). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate labeling as exploratory with weaker effects. Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge, acknowledging exploratory nature as appropriate.

Strong agreement on state-dependence conclusion (C14-C15, C143). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes longitudinal data support this interpretation; peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence' for state-dependency and note it advances understanding beyond cross-sectional studies.

Agreement on specificity controls (C74-C75). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these analyses address baseline confounding; peer reviewers acknowledge thorough examination of specificity with appropriate analyses.

Agreement on sample size limitations (C137-C139). Both rate as SUPPORTED acknowledgment of limitation. OpenEval notes small samples in non-iCBT arms limit power; peer reviewers explicitly state antidepressant and control groups were underpowered, reducing generalizability.

Partial overlap on treatment non-specificity (C95, C121). Both rate UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes non-significant three-way interaction and underpowered comparisons; peer reviewers question whether effect is truly treatment-specific given lack of interaction with treatment.

Agreement on temporal limitation (C130-C131). Both rate as SUPPORTED acknowledgment. OpenEval notes lack of continuous assessment prevents causal inference; peer reviewers note two timepoints prevent determining if confidence changes drive treatment effects.

Partial overlap on specificity to anxious-depression (C71-C72). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes lack of association with compulsivity change strengthens specificity; peer reviewers acknowledge thorough examination of specificity without challenge.

Agreement on small effect size acknowledgment (C125). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for appropriate caveats about weak correlation and limited clinical utility. Peer reviewers similarly emphasize small effects call clinical relevance into question.
OpenEval evaluates background literature and knowledge gap (C1-C2, C28-C31) as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory claims.

OpenEval evaluates study design and methodology (C3-C5, C39, C46-C47, C144-C145, C152-C153, C155, C157) as SUPPORTED with clear documentation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological claims.
OpenEval evaluates demographic and task correlates at baseline (C51-C57) as SUPPORTED with adequate power. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these baseline correlate findings.

OpenEval evaluates metacognitive task methodology (C177-C184) as SUPPORTED, noting validation and high reliability as methodological strength. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these task description claims.
